strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: feed-forward construction of language-embedded 3D Gaussian scenes from unposed multi-view images. Combining reconstruction, novel-view synthesis, open-vocabulary querying, and editing in one representation would be valuable for robotics, AR/VR, and data generation if robustly realized.

The proposed system is technically plausible and well motivated. The use of VGGT-derived pseudo geometry, novel-view photometric supervision, CLIP/SAM-based instance supervision, instance-guided contrastive learning, and geometry/semantic sparsification forms a coherent pipeline for lifting 2D semantic information into a 3D Gaussian representation without requiring explicit 3D labels during training.

The quantitative results show large gains over feed-forward baselines on ScanNet across 2, 8, 16, and 32 input views, with improvements in both NVS metrics and open-vocabulary segmentation metrics. The comparison to per-scene optimization methods also suggests a strong efficiency advantage.

The hierarchical sparsification idea is a useful engineering contribution: separating dense geometry Gaussians from sparser semantic Gaussians is natural and could reduce memory/runtime overhead while preserving semantic coverage.
The paper is generally clear, with a readable architecture/training description and enough high-level implementation detail to understand the major components.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is narrower than the claims. The method is claimed to work from 'any views' and to generalize from sparse to dense settings, but evaluation is mainly on indoor ScanNet/ScanNet++ scenes with selected view counts. There is little evidence for robustness to wider baselines, outdoor videos, dynamic content, severe occlusion, domain shift, or arbitrary video sources, despite the training-data claims.

The comparison protocol raises fairness questions. Several baselines are adapted via post-processing because they only accept fixed view counts, while FLEG is designed for variable views; this may disadvantage baselines in dense-view settings. The per-scene optimization comparison reports only semantic metrics and time, without reconstruction quality, hardware details, or careful tuning discussion.

The '3D-annotation-free' framing is somewhat overstated. The method heavily depends on a pretrained 3D foundation model for pseudo point maps/cameras, and InstanceMV-14K partly uses scan datasets with 3D annotations to obtain masks. This is still a useful weak-supervision recipe, but the claim should be qualified more carefully.

Ablations are too limited for a system with many interacting components. There is no detailed ablation of novel-view selection, CLIP feature aggregation, SAM2 mask quality, training data sources, number of input views during training, semantic voxel size, memory/runtime tradeoffs, or the contribution of pretrained VGGT initialization versus the proposed losses.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper does not specify enough details about dataset construction, train/test splits, instance-mask generation settings, CLIP variant, Gaussian counts, rendering resolution, hardware, batch size, training duration, or whether InstanceMV-14K and code will be released. The project page field is blank in the manuscript.

The semantic evaluation is limited to open-vocabulary segmentation metrics derived from language queries, but the paper also claims 3D editing and downstream real-time applicability. Editing is shown qualitatively but not evaluated, and there is no user-facing or task-level validation for robotics/AR-style use cases.

Some important limitations are not discussed, such as dependence on pseudo-pose quality, failure modes when VGGT predictions are wrong, semantic inconsistency from CLIP/SAM supervision, scaling to very large scenes, and memory/runtime behavior for dense high-resolution inputs.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: fast construction of language-embedded 3D Gaussian scenes from unposed multi-view images, with support for both sparse and denser view settings.

The proposed system is practically motivated. Combining feed-forward reconstruction, language-aligned features, and Gaussian representations could be valuable for interactive 3D query/editing if convincingly validated.

The manuscript presents several plausible engineering components, including VGGT-based pseudo-supervision, instance-guided contrastive learning, and geometry/semantic sparsification, and reports improvements over selected language-field baselines in both semantic query and rendering metrics.
weaknesses: The core novelty is limited and the method appears heavily dependent on VGGT: the transformer, camera/depth heads, initialization, pseudo camera/depth labels, and training target selection all rely on VGGT. The paper does not sufficiently disentangle what is learned by FLEG from what is inherited or distilled from the pretrained 3D foundation model.

The experimental evidence is not convincing enough for the breadth of the claims. Evaluation is limited mainly to ScanNet/ScanNet++, while the paper claims arbitrary uncalibrated/unposed inputs, sparse-to-dense robustness, real-time downstream applicability, and broad generalization. Outdoor scenes, object-centric scenes, in-the-wild videos, failure cases, and cross-dataset generalization are missing.

There is a serious potential data leakage concern. InstanceMV-14K is built from ScanNet and ScanNet++, and the evaluations/ablations are also on ScanNet and ScanNet++. The paper does not clearly specify train/test scene splits or whether evaluation scenes are excluded from the constructed training corpus.

The baseline comparison is weak. Important feed-forward reconstruction/NVS baselines such as AnySplat are cited but not quantitatively compared. Existing fixed-view methods are adapted with post-processing for larger view counts, which may strongly handicap them and makes the dense-view comparison difficult to interpret.

The comparison with per-scene optimization methods is incomplete: Table 2 reports only semantic metrics and time, omitting reconstruction metrics, although the paper claims joint high-fidelity geometry/appearance and semantic embedding. Conversely, the feed-forward table mixes LSeg, which has no NVS capability and uses ground-truth novel views, with 3D reconstruction methods.

Ablations are too shallow for a system with many moving parts. The paper lacks ablations for the dataset composition, pseudo-label quality, target-view selection threshold, CLIP aggregation, semantic voxel size, number of input views during training, feature dimensionality, and the claimed geometry-semantic hierarchical sparsification beyond a single embedding-count row.

Reproducibility is poor. Key implementation details are missing or underspecified, including dataset splits, exact sampling protocol, voxel sizes, semantic feature dimension, SH degree, coverage threshold, training schedule/compute, batch size, number of iterations, data filtering, SAM2 mask generation details, and whether code/data will be released. The project-page line is empty.

The claim of being 3D-annotation-free is somewhat overstated: the method uses VGGT-predicted point maps and camera poses as pseudo 3D supervision, and parts of the dataset derive masks from 3D-annotated ScanNet/ScanNet++. The paper should frame this more carefully as pseudo-3D/self-supervised training rather than simply annotation-free.

The presentation contains imprecise or possibly erroneous technical details, e.g. the semantic voxel size is described as smaller while the goal is a sparser semantic set, and several equations/definitions are underspecified. These issues make it hard to verify the method from the manuscript alone.

The paper does not discuss limitations, failure modes, societal considerations, or risks from relying on CLIP/SAM2 pseudo-labels and internet video data. This is especially important for language-grounded 3D representations where semantic bias and incorrect object grounding can propagate into downstream robotics or AR applications.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: feed-forward construction of language-embedded 3D Gaussian representations from unposed, uncalibrated multi-view images. The target setting is practically meaningful because existing language-field methods are often per-scene optimized, slow, or constrained to fixed sparse-view inputs.

The proposed system is technically well motivated. Combining VGGT-style feed-forward geometry, novel-view photometric supervision from pseudo poses/point maps, CLIP/SAM-derived instance supervision, instance-guided contrastive learning, and geometry-semantic sparsification forms a coherent pipeline for jointly handling reconstruction and open-vocabulary semantics.

The empirical results are strong within the evaluated setting. On ScanNet, FLEG substantially improves over feed-forward baselines across 2, 8, 16, and 32 input views for both reconstruction metrics and semantic metrics, and remains stable as the number of views increases. The comparison to per-scene language-Gaussian methods also shows a compelling runtime advantage with better reported open-vocabulary segmentation accuracy.
The paper’s qualitative figures support the quantitative claims: the outputs appear sharper than competing feed-forward methods and the semantic query maps are visibly cleaner in the shown examples.

The method includes useful component-level ideas beyond simple system integration, especially instance-guided contrastive alignment and semantic Gaussian sparsification. The ablations, though limited, indicate that geometry distillation, instance contrastive loss, and sparsification each contribute to the final behavior.
weaknesses: The claim of being “3D-annotation-free” needs more nuance. The method depends heavily on VGGT pseudo geometry and camera estimates, and VGGT itself was trained with 3D/geometric supervision. This is a reasonable distillation strategy, but the paper’s wording risks overstating independence from 3D supervision.

The experimental scope is narrower than the claims. Evaluation is limited mainly to ScanNet/ScanNet++, i.e., indoor scenes closely related to some training sources. The paper claims arbitrary views and broad downstream potential, but does not sufficiently test outdoor scenes, object-centric data, in-the-wild videos, severe camera motion, dynamic content, or domain transfer.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a 1B-parameter system trained on a 15M-image InstanceMV-14K dataset. The paper does not specify training compute, schedule length, batch size, sampling details, dataset filtering, SAM2/CLIP variants, or whether the dataset/model/code will be released. These omissions make independent verification difficult.

The baseline comparison is plausible but not fully airtight. Some baselines are adapted with post-processing to handle view counts outside their natural setting, while stronger feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction baselines without semantics are not used to contextualize the NVS gains. The per-scene baselines are evaluated only on semantic metrics in Table 2, without reconstruction metrics under the same dense-view setting.

The ablations are too sparse for the number of proposed components. There is no detailed ablation of novel-view selection thresholding, 3D feature aggregation, dataset scale/source composition, semantic voxel size, confidence weighting, or the effect of VGGT initialization versus architecture/training choices.

The paper gives little discussion of failure cases and limitations. Important issues such as SAM/CLIP label noise, inherited VGGT geometric errors, memory usage of the 1B-parameter model, behavior under occlusion or very sparse overlap, and risks of biased semantic embeddings are not analyzed.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: feed-forward reconstruction of language-embedded 3D Gaussians from unposed, uncalibrated, variable-number multi-view inputs. This is a meaningful step beyond two-view or pose-dependent semantic Gaussian methods.

The proposed combination of VGGT-based geometric distillation, novel-view supervision, CLIP/SAM2 semantic distillation, and instance-guided contrastive learning is technically coherent and well matched to the stated goal of avoiding 3D ground-truth geometry and semantic labels.

The decoupled sparse semantic Gaussian representation is a strong practical contribution. The ablations show that it reduces language-embedding storage dramatically, e.g. about 18 MB versus 397-491 MB, while maintaining comparable mIoU/mAcc.

Experimental coverage is broad: ScanNet++, ScanNet, 2/4/8/16/32-view settings, feed-forward and per-scene baselines, ablations, camera pose/depth analyses, and an unseen Replica evaluation. The reported gains over language-embedded feed-forward baselines are substantial, especially for semantic segmentation.
The limitations section is unusually candid about dependence on VGGT, indoor-scene generalization, and memory scaling to hundreds or thousands of images.
weaknesses: The method's novelty is somewhat entangled with a large pretrained 3D foundation model: the architecture initializes from VGGT and distills VGGT geometry/camera predictions. This is a reasonable engineering choice, but it weakens the claim that the method independently solves pose-free geometry; some gains may largely reflect VGGT plus added heads and losses.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing for variable-view comparisons. LSM and Uni3R are evaluated with their official two-view models by selecting the nearest two views even in 4/8/16-view settings, while FLEG consumes all views. This is disclosed, but it makes the multi-view superiority claims less clean.

The semantic evaluation relies on open-vocabulary query segmentation metrics, but the manuscript gives limited detail on query construction, class sets, thresholds, mask post-processing, and how CLIP/SAM2-derived training signals overlap with evaluation categories. This affects reproducibility and the interpretation of semantic gains.

The 32-view comparison with per-scene optimized methods is performed on a subset because of optimization cost, while the main feed-forward comparison uses full validation sets. The subset selection protocol is only briefly described, leaving some risk of selection bias.

The experimental evidence is mostly indoor-centric. Replica generalization helps, but all datasets are indoor scenes, so the claimed broader applicability to embodied systems, AR/VR, and large-scale assets remains only partially supported.

The paper would benefit from runtime and memory measurements at inference, especially because scalability and feed-forward practicality are central claims. The 1B-parameter model and added language embeddings may be expensive despite reduced storage for reconstructed assets.

Some presentation issues reduce polish and reproducibility: several equations/paragraphs are hard to parse in the extracted manuscript, Table 2 appears to contain a typo such as '0.79.74', and the project page/code availability is left unspecified.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: feed-forward reconstruction of language-embedded 3D Gaussian scenes from unposed multi-view images, with support for variable numbers of input views.

The proposed compact semantic Gaussian representation is a sensible idea, and the ablation suggests that dense per-Gaussian language embeddings are highly redundant: storage drops from hundreds of MB to about 18 MB with little semantic degradation.

The manuscript includes comparisons across reconstruction and open-vocabulary segmentation metrics on ScanNet, ScanNet++, and an unseen Replica setting, plus ablations for sparse semantics, contrastive learning, and novel-view distillation.

The system is practically attractive if the reported results hold: it combines geometry, appearance, and language querying/editing in one feed-forward pipeline rather than requiring per-scene optimization.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat limited. The method largely combines strong existing components, especially VGGT, SAM2, CLIP, Gaussian splatting, voxel aggregation, and standard distillation losses. The paper does not fully disentangle how much improvement comes from the proposed ideas versus inheriting VGGT's geometry and camera estimation ability.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness concerns. Several key baselines are restricted to two views even in 4/8/16-view settings, while FLEG can consume all views. This supports the practical claim, but it also makes the numerical advantage hard to interpret as an algorithmic improvement over comparable multi-view methods.

The paper makes strong claims about arbitrary views, pose-free inference, and scalable/real-time applicability, but it reports little about inference time, GPU memory, scaling with many views, failure modes, or robustness to outdoor/diverse scenes. The method has around 1B parameters and still requires additional language embeddings, so the deployment claims are under-supported.

The semantic evaluation needs more detail and scrutiny. The model is trained from SAM2+CLIP pseudo-labels and then compared against SAM2+CLIP and LSeg, but the paper does not sufficiently explain prompt sets, label mapping, query selection, mask generation details, or whether evaluation choices favor the proposed distillation setup.

The 32-view comparison with per-scene optimized language-GS methods is not fully convincing. It is performed on a validation subset for expensive baselines, while the exact subset, optimization settings, and comparability are not adequately specified. Table 2 also contains an apparent invalid SSIM value, which weakens confidence in experimental care.

The ablations are useful but incomplete. There is no clear comparison isolating VGGT initialization versus VGGT distillation, no analysis of sensitivity to SAM2 mask errors, no runtime/storage tradeoff beyond embedding storage, and no statistical variation across scenes or random view sampling.

The manuscript has clarity and reproducibility gaps: some equations/text are awkward, implementation details such as voxel sizes and training data sampling are incomplete in the main paper, and the project page/code availability is left unspecified. These issues do not invalidate the idea, but they make the empirical case less reliable.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: feed-forward reconstruction of language-embedded 3D Gaussians from arbitrary unposed multi-view images. This is a meaningful step beyond two-view or pose-dependent language-Gaussian methods, and the contribution is well aligned with current computer vision interests in 3D reconstruction, open-vocabulary scene understanding, and efficient 3D representations.

The proposed dual-branch distillation framework is technically sensible. Leveraging VGGT for geometry/camera pseudo-supervision, SAM2/CLIP for semantic distillation, and adding novel-view-based supervision forms a coherent training recipe that avoids requiring 3D ground truth or semantic labels.

The Decoupled Gaussian Language Embedding module is a strong practical contribution. The paper makes a convincing case that dense per-Gaussian language features are redundant, and the ablations show a large storage reduction, from hundreds of MB to about 18 MB, with comparable or better semantic accuracy.

The experimental results are broad within the chosen setting. The method is compared against feed-forward reconstruction, feed-forward language-embedded Gaussian, 2D open-vocabulary segmentation, and per-scene optimized language-Gaussian baselines on ScanNet++ and ScanNet, with an additional Replica generalization study. Results consistently support the main claims.

The ablation study is useful and directly tied to the paper’s design choices: sparse semantic Gaussians, instance-guided contrastive learning, novel-view distillation, and geometric distillation each have measurable effects.
The paper is generally clear and well structured, with qualitative results that make the improvements in novel-view synthesis and open-vocabulary querying easy to understand.
weaknesses: The evidence is still concentrated on indoor RGB-D-style datasets. Although Replica is used for cross-dataset evaluation, all experiments remain indoor-scene focused, so the claim of scalable arbitrary multi-view training and broad deployment is not yet fully demonstrated for outdoor, object-centric, dynamic, or in-the-wild captures.

The method relies heavily on large pretrained systems: VGGT, DINOv2, SAM2, and CLIP. This is a reasonable engineering choice, but it makes the novelty partly a strong integration/distillation pipeline rather than a fully independent reconstruction approach. The paper could better disentangle which gains come from FLEG-specific ideas versus inherited capabilities of these foundation models.

The efficiency story is incomplete. The paper emphasizes feed-forward inference and compact storage, but it uses a roughly 1B-parameter model and does not report runtime, inference memory, throughput, or scaling with the number of input views. This is important because the intended applications include real-time embodied perception and large-scale asset construction.

Some comparisons are imperfect. For LSM and Uni3R, the official two-view models are used even in multi-view settings by selecting nearest views, while FLEG can consume all views. This is understandable, but it weakens the strength of conclusions about arbitrary-view superiority over architectures not designed for this setting.

The quantitative behavior with increasing input views is somewhat surprising in places, with reconstruction metrics often degrading from 2 to 16 views. The paper attributes related issues to view selection/evaluation only indirectly; a clearer analysis would help readers understand whether this reflects dataset protocol, occlusions, model capacity, or limitations in multi-view aggregation.

Reproducibility details are moderate but not complete. Important implementation choices such as thresholds for novel-view selection, voxel sizes beyond the default semantic sparsity discussion, sampling details, exact CLIP/SAM2 settings, runtime costs, and release plans are not sufficiently emphasized in the main paper.

There are small presentation issues, including a likely typo in Table 2 for ScanNet LangSplat SSIM reported as 0.79.74, and the project page field appears blank in the extracted manuscript. These do not undermine the core contribution but should be corrected.
